subchapters.title: Physical quantities and units
subchapters.theory: A physical quantity is a measurable property expressed as a numerical value multiplied by a unit. SI uses seven base quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Derived quantities are formed algebraically from base quantities.
key_points: A measurement has magnitude and unit.
SI base units are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.
Units must be consistent before using equations.
derivations: Choose the appropriate base quantities for the quantity.
Write its defining relation in SI base quantities.
Collect powers of M, L, T and other dimensions.
subchapters.examples: A length of 2.50 m is written with a numerical value and the unit metre; the unit does not change the physical quantity.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct about Physical quantities and units?
options: A measurement has magnitude and unit.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Physical quantities and units.

revision: A measurement has magnitude and unit.
SI base units are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.
Units must be consistent before using equations.
Core formula: [Q] = M^a L^b T^c ...

subchapters.title: SI units
subchapters.theory: The SI system provides a coherent set of units. Base units generate derived units such as newton, joule, pascal and watt. Prefixes such as kilo, milli and micro represent powers of ten.
key_points: Newton is kg m s^-2.
Joule is kg m^2 s^-2.
Prefixes must be converted before calculation.
derivations: Start from the SI definition of the derived quantity.
Substitute the base units.
Simplify the powers of base units.
subchapters.examples: Convert 5 cm to SI: 5 cm = 5×10^-2 m = 0.05 m.

options: Newton is kg m s^-2.

The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of SI units.

revision: Newton is kg m s^-2.
Joule is kg m^2 s^-2.
Prefixes must be converted before calculation.
Core formula: 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2

subchapters.title: Dimensions and dimensional analysis
subchapters.theory: Dimensional analysis represents a quantity using powers of fundamental dimensions. It checks dimensional consistency, helps derive relations up to a dimensionless constant, and converts units. It cannot determine numerical constants such as 2 or π.
key_points: Every term added in a physical equation must have the same dimensions.
A dimensionally correct equation is not necessarily physically correct.
Arguments of trigonometric functions must be dimensionless.
derivations: Write the proposed relation.
Replace each variable by its dimensions.
Equate powers of each fundamental dimension.
subchapters.examples: For s = ut + 1/2 at^2, both ut and at^2 have dimensions of length, so the equation is dimensionally consistent.

mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Dimensions and dimensional analysis.

revision: Every term added in a physical equation must have the same dimensions.

Arguments of trigonometric functions must be dimensionless.
Core formula: [v] = LT^-1

subchapters.title: Significant figures
subchapters.theory: Significant figures indicate the precision justified by a measurement. Non-zero digits are significant; captive zeros are significant; leading zeros are not. In multiplication and division, the result is limited by the least number of significant figures; in addition and subtraction, by the least decimal places.
key_points: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
Do not round intermediate values too early.
derivations: Count significant digits according to the measurement rules.
Perform the operation without premature rounding.
Round the final answer to the required precision.
subchapters.examples: 2.50 has three significant figures, while 0.00250 also has three significant figures.

options: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
The topic has no measurable physical quantities.
SI units are never required in numerical problems.
The governing physical law can be ignored.
mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Significant figures.

revision: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
Do not round intermediate values too early.
Core formula: % uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty/measured value)×100

subchapters.title: Errors in measurement
subchapters.theory: Measurement error is the difference between a measured value and the accepted or true value. Random errors vary between trials; systematic errors shift measurements in a consistent way. Uncertainty is often expressed as absolute, relative or percentage uncertainty.
key_points: Absolute error has the same unit as the measured quantity.
Relative error is dimensionless.
For addition/subtraction, absolute uncertainties add; for products/quotients, fractional uncertainties add approximately.
derivations: Find the absolute uncertainty in each measured quantity.
Convert to fractional uncertainty when products or powers are involved.
Multiply by 100 for percentage uncertainty.

mcqs.explanation: The correct choice follows from the definition and governing principles of Errors in measurement.

revision: Absolute error has the same unit as the measured quantity.

For addition/subtraction, absolute uncertainties add; for products/quotients, fractional uncertainties add approximately.
Core formula: Δx/x

subchapters.title: Vernier calipers
subchapters.theory: A Vernier caliper measures external diameter, internal diameter and depth more precisely than a simple scale. Its least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division. A corrected reading must account for zero error.
key_points: Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD.
Reading = main-scale reading + Vernier coincidence × least count.
Zero correction is the negative of zero error.
derivations: Read the main scale just before the Vernier zero.
Find the coinciding Vernier division.
Multiply the coincidence by least count and apply zero correction.
subchapters.examples: If MSR = 2.3 cm, VC = 6 and LC = 0.01 cm, observed reading = 2.36 cm before zero correction.

revision: Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD.

Zero correction is the negative of zero error.
Core formula: MSR + VC×LC

subchapters.title: Screw gauge
subchapters.theory: A screw gauge uses the pitch of a screw and a circular scale to measure small thicknesses and diameters. Pitch is the axial distance moved in one complete rotation. Least count equals pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.
key_points: Pitch = distance moved/number of rotations.
Least count = pitch/number of circular divisions.
Apply zero correction to the observed reading.
derivations: Determine pitch from one or more rotations.
Calculate least count.
Add pitch-scale and circular-scale readings and apply zero correction.
subchapters.examples: Pitch 1 mm with 100 circular divisions gives LC = 0.01 mm.
